passage: Sunday, 11 pm. Uma didn't say a word when I got home at ten again, just kept the book open on the same page. Then: "I had dinner alone four times this week." I started to defend myself, the launch, the deadline, and stopped. I could hear how it sounded. It's true, and I hadn't noticed the days piling up until Uma counted them. I'm not proud. I don't want resentment to set in before I fix it. So tonight I said my laptop closes at seven on weekdays, no exceptions unless it's a real emergency, and we're taking Saturday to go to the lake, phones off. Uma smiled a little. The work matters, but what's it worth if the flat feels empty when I'm in it? — Pankaj

qa.q: At what time will Pankaj's laptop close on weekdays?
How did Pankaj feel on stopping in the middle of defending, and why?
qa.a: Pankaj felt ashamed, writing "I'm not proud", after hearing how the excuses sounded and realising what Uma said was true.

qa.q: What could Pankaj do to make the shut-off time hold?
qa.a: Keep it consistently, tell the team about it, be fully present at home and keep the Saturday plan for the lake.

qa.q: How might Uma have felt through the week of lone dinners?
qa.a: Alone and quiet, judging by the unturned page and the count of dinners. The small smile suggests some hope.

grounding: Work swallows the evenings and the partner feels alone; noticing it early, setting a shut-off time, planning a shared day and being present.

passage:
Ganga had a product launch in six days, and her team was two people short. She'd been leaving the flat in Hyderabad at seven and coming home at eleven for a month.

Tonight, walking in, she found Rekha asleep on the sofa. A plate covered with another plate sat on the table. Next to it, Rekha's phone showed a message Rekha had typed to a friend and never sent: "I feel like I'm married to a ghost."

Ganga stood there a long time. She'd been so focused on the launch she hadn't noticed.

She sat on the floor by the sofa. When Rekha woke, Ganga said, "I saw the message. I'm sorry. You're right."

"The launch..." Rekha began.

"Six days. I can't skip them. But from Monday, laptop off at eight, every night. And after the launch, the whole Sunday is ours. The lake, the old café."

Rekha squeezed her hand. "Just come home with your head too."

"I'll try. Tell me if I don't."

qa.q: How many days were left before the product launch?
What was Ganga feeling as she stood reading Rekha's unsent message?
qa.a: Ganga felt shocked and guilty, realising she had been too focused on the launch to notice Rekha's loneliness.

qa.q: What steps did Ganga commit to, and why do they help?
qa.a: A laptop-off time of eight from Monday and a shared Sunday after the launch, which protect time together before resentment builds.

qa.q: How does Rekha see Ganga's long hours?
qa.a: Rekha feels alone, as if married to a ghost, and wants Ganga present in mind as well as body.

grounding: Under the pressure of a launch with a short-staffed team, the passage shows someone whose work has swallowed her evenings, noticing her partner's loneliness and setting a shut-off time and a shared day.

passage:
It was Sarita's birthday, and Usha remembered at 9:40 p.m., still at her desk in the Andheri office.

She got home at eleven with a supermarket cake. Sarita was on the balcony, not crying, just quiet. "It's fine," she said, in the flat voice that meant it wasn't.

Usha sat down beside her. For months she'd been proud of her promotion, her late nights, the praise. She'd been telling herself it was all for their future. Looking at Sarita's face, she saw the future had been sitting alone on this balcony most evenings.

"It's not fine," Usha said. "I've been gone. Even when I'm here, I'm on my phone."

Sarita looked at her. "I miss you."

"I know. I'm setting a rule. Office laptop shuts at seven. Phone goes in the drawer at dinner. And this Saturday, you choose. Anything."

"The old bookshop and street food," Sarita said. "Like when we first met."

"Done," Usha said, and put her phone in her pocket, face down.

qa.q: What time did Usha remember Sarita's birthday?
What did Usha feel looking at Sarita on the balcony?
qa.a: Usha felt guilty and sad, realising her ambition had left Sarita alone most evenings.

qa.q: What did Usha change, and why is it a good step?
qa.a: She set a seven o'clock laptop shut-off, no phone at dinner, and a shared Saturday of Sarita's choosing, to be present before resentment grows.

qa.q: How does Sarita experience Usha's long hours?
qa.a: Sarita feels lonely and missed, saying "It's fine" in a flat voice while clearly hurt.

grounding: The passage shows someone whose work has swallowed her evenings and left her partner alone, and who sets a shut-off time, plans a shared day and chooses to be present.
